Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00709

In thought, by contrast, considering the essence alone means setting aside both existence and nonexistence. In Avicenna's phrase “it would have no existence if it stood alone,” the word “no” expresses a simple denial; it does not describe a positive state of having no existence. The commentator then explains how to read the wording.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00710

Once you understand what we said earlier about how an essence is described as existing, and how the principle that a predicate depends on its subject can be made sound, the meaning of essential coming-to-be and the priority of an essence to its existence should be clear. For one thing to come before another, the first must have some kind of presence that the second does not yet have. If essential coming-to-be means that an essence comes before its existence, we must give the essence some prior state of existence. Yet any way of considering the essence, whether as existing or not existing, seems to give it some kind of existence. How, then, can it come before its own existence?
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00711

There is only one way to understand this. The mind can set aside an essence's particular existence and all other forms of existence, then describe it as having its own existence. In this way, the essence comes before existence in general. But this act of setting it apart is itself a kind of existence. In one respect, the essence is nonexistent under this way of considering it, so it comes after existence in general. In another respect, it has existence under this very consideration, and so it can be said to come before existence through existence. The same is true of a capacity becoming active in prime matter: in one respect it is nonexistent, and in another it has a kind of existence as a capacity.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00712

The second argument says that the essence of every possible thing differs from its existence. If its existence came from its essence, the essence would have to exist before it existed. So its existence must come from something else. Whatever receives existence from something else is preceded by that other thing in an essential sense; therefore, it has come to be essentially. This also shows that what is eternal in itself has no essence. The objections raised by al-Rāzī have already been answered.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00713

Neither argument applies to existence itself, which is made by God and is, in itself, an effect of the Necessary Being. We have said that existence has another kind of dependence and so another kind of coming-to-be: essential poverty, meaning that a thing depends on its maker in its very being. Put another way, whatever exists depends on something else for its existence. An essence, considered simply as an essence, does not depend on a maker; nor does it exist on its own as an essence. So it is neither eternal nor originated in this sense. Only God is free of this dependence. We may use “eternal” and “originated” in this way, even though philosophers do not commonly use the terms like this.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00714
III. Is Coming-to-Be in Time an Extra Feature of Existence?
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00715

A scholar says that a thing's coming-to-be is neither its existence now—otherwise everything that exists would have come to be—nor its earlier nonexistence considered just as nonexistence—otherwise every nonexistence would count as coming-to-be. Instead, coming-to-be means that a thing is preceded by nonexistence. It is an extra feature, added to the thing's existence and nonexistence. The scholar then asks: Is this feature itself something that came to be? If so, its own coming-to-be would be another added feature, and this would go on without end. If it did not come to be, then the coming-to-be of the thing would have to be eternal, which is impossible. The reply is that, just as existence exists through itself, coming-to-be comes to be through itself.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00716

I say that the beginning of this scholar's argument contradicts its end. If coming-to-be were a quality added to the thing's existence and nonexistence, that quality would have its own nature within the category of qualities, and an existence added to that nature. If its existence is added to its nature, its coming-to-be would also be added to its nature and existence, since the meaning of coming-to-be is not the same as the nature of a quality. How, then, could coming-to-be be identical with that quality?
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00717

Also, coming-to-be applies to every category of thing. A quality comes to be in one way; a substance, quantity, and other kinds of thing come to be in their own ways. There cannot be one fixed quality, neither a relation nor something made up of parts, that applies to every kind of thing that comes to be, while changing its meaning only according to what it is related to. Relations work in that way; coming-to-be does not. Existence, too, differs with the natures of things, as we have explained. Yet it is not an extra feature added to them in the world outside thought. It is their existence.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00718

The scholar's view also implies that a newly arisen nonexistence has an extra positive quality of its own. The truth is that the idea of coming-to-be is conceptually distinct from existence, but it is identical with the particular existences of things that come to be and pass away. Those things are coming-to-be through their own individual existence. Their coming-to-be is not what the agent makes; their existence is. Existence is what is made in itself, not the description “coming-to-be.” Being preceded by nonexistence belongs to that existence by its own nature; it is not caused by something else. Like existence and individuation in general, coming-to-be is one broad concept that applies in different degrees. It covers many distinct kinds of coming-to-be, for which we have no established names. We can only call them “this kind of coming-to-be” or “that kind,” as we learned in the discussion of existence.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00719
IV. Coming-to-Be and the Need for a Cause
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00720

Coming-to-be is not, in itself, why things need a cause that brings them into existence. If it were, the essences of created things would not need a cause. But they do: because they are possible and neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary for them, they must have a cause that brings them into existence. Neither of two equally open alternatives can prevail without something to decide between them.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00721

The philosophers say that coming-to-be means a thing's existence is preceded by nonexistence. They treat this as a feature that follows the thing's existence. But the thing's existence comes after the cause has acted, and the cause acts only after the thing has some reason to need a cause. So coming-to-be cannot be the reason for this need, or a condition or part of that reason. Otherwise, it would have to come before itself by several steps, which is impossible.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00722

I say that calling coming-to-be a feature that follows existence is loose wording. As we have seen, coming-to-be is not a feature added to the existence of something that has come to be. We have also seen that each thing's existence at a particular level includes its being at that level. But this does not weaken the point. A thing that has come to be certainly needs a cause. The need must come either from its possibility or, in some way, from its coming-to-be. If we imagined both removed, the thing would be necessary and eternal, and so would not need a cause. Since we have ruled out coming-to-be as the source of the need, only possibility remains. The truth, however, is that the need for a cause comes from neither of these. It comes from the fact that a thing's existence depends on, and is held up by, something else.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00723

The claim that an essence's possibility comes before its existence is correct when we consider the essence in itself. But existence comes before essence in the order of reality, as an actual thing comes before what is only potential, and form before matter. Until there is existence, no essence is realized at all. As we have said, existence is also what makes a thing this particular thing; nothing exists without becoming a particular. Possibility comes after essence because it is a feature of essence. How, then, can possibility be the cause of existence when, by supposition, possibility comes after existence itself?
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00724

The familiar argument—“it was possible, so it needed a cause, and then it came to exist”—is sound when we consider the essence as the mind sets it apart from existence. We do not deny that an essence's possibility explains why it needs a cause in that way. Its possibility comes before its existence, meaning before it is described as existing. This description takes place in thought, even though the existence we are describing is real.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00725

Coming-to-be does, however, give rise to a need for a preparatory cause, and such a cause is only an incidental cause. Every thing that comes to be is preceded by a possibility of existence. This possibility is itself something real, not merely an idea in the mind. It has degrees of strength and weakness, and can be near to its result or far from it. A near possibility is readiness; a more distant one is capacity.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00726

This possibility must either be a substance or an accident. It cannot be a substance that exists entirely on its own, since then it would not belong to anything. Nor would there be any reason for one thing, rather than any other, to have the same independent possibility. So the possibility of a thing that comes to be must have a bearer. It may be a form in matter or an accident in a subject. In either case, it comes before the thing in time and ends when that thing exists.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00727

The bearer of this possibility must be connected to the thing that comes to be. Otherwise, there would be no reason why it was the possibility of this thing rather than another. The bearer of its capacity and possibility must be the very bearer of its existence, the bearer of one of its parts, or the bearer of something that exists along with it. So although this possibility is itself real, it is the nonexistence of the thing that is to come to be, and its capacity to become that thing. It cannot exist at the same time as the thing's actual existence. This is why some ancient thinkers counted nonexistence among the causes of a thing that comes to be. They therefore counted five causes: nonexistence, the agent, the end, the matter, and the form.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00728
The truth is that nonexistence is not a direct cause, but an incidental one.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00729

If it were a direct cause, it would not disappear when the thing came into existence. The matter that carries the thing's possibility, by contrast, is one of its direct causes. Also, the priority of nonexistence to existence is priority in time. This is the same as the priority of earlier parts of time over later ones. So nonexistence comes first only incidentally, not in itself. Perhaps the ancients counted nonexistence as a direct cause because what comes to be in time is, in reality, made up of parts of motion and time. These have a weak kind of existence: as each part or instance passes away, another part or instance comes into being. From this point of view, nonexistence can be called a direct cause of what comes to be.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00730
V. Ways One Thing Can Come Before Another
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00731

Priority and posteriority are among the features of anything that exists. There are several kinds of priority: priority in rank, in nature, in excellence, in time, and in essence or causation. There are also two more kinds, which we will explain.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00732

Priority in rank means that whatever is closer to an actual or assumed starting point comes first. For example, Baghdad may be said to come before Kufa. There are two kinds of this rank. One follows the natural order of things, though it is not priority by nature in the technical sense: a body comes before an animal, and an animal before a human being. The other follows a chosen order or position in space. For example, the row nearest the prayer leader comes before the next row, if we take the prayer niche as our starting point.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00733

Priority in rank can be reversed: what came first can become last, and what came last can become first, if we choose a new starting point. If we make the human being the starting point, whatever is closer to a human being comes first. On this basis, a human being would come before a body, even before a substance. In the earlier example, a worshipper comes before the prayer leader when we count from the door toward the prayer niche.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00734

Natural rank appears in every chain that is ordered by the nature of its members rather than by a chosen arrangement. This includes causes and effects, qualities and the things that have them, and kinds arranged from broader to narrower. If you move upward from the lowest effect, you eventually reach the highest cause. If you move downward, the highest comes first. The same applies to the broadest kinds, the most specific kinds, and other ordered series. Philosophers base their proof against an infinite chain on such series when their members exist together.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00735

Priority by nature is like the priority of one over two, or of a line over a triangle. Remove what comes later, and what came before it can still remain; remove what came before, and what came after it cannot remain. The measure of this priority is whether something can exist, not whether it must exist.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00736

Priority by causation means that the existence of what comes first causes the existence of what comes later. The cause comes before its effect both in existence and in necessity, because the cause makes the effect necessary. Priority by excellence or honor is what we mean when we say that Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, comes before the other prophets. Priority in time is familiar. The earlier thing does not exist at the same time as the later one. This differs from priority by nature, where the earlier thing can exist together with the later one.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00737

Anyone who says that the agent makes the very essence of a thing, rather than its existence, and that the agent's own essence, rather than its existence, is what acts, must add another kind: priority by essence. The same is true of anyone who says that a possible thing's essence comes before its existence simply as an essence, without considering any kind of existence.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00738

Of the two further kinds of priority I mentioned, the first is priority in reality. Existence comes before the essence that exists through it, because existence is, in our view, what truly makes something exist. The essence exists through existence in a secondary sense. The same is true of two things that share a feature such as motion, position, or quantity, when one has the feature directly and the other only through its relation to the first. The first comes before the second in this further sense.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00739

This is different from priority by excellence, since what comes later in excellence must still possess some share of the quality in which it is surpassed. It also differs from priority by nature and by causation, since in those kinds the later thing shares something with the earlier one. This further kind of priority is plainly different from priority in time or rank.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00740

You might ask: in each kind of priority, what is the feature that makes the first thing prior and the second later? What makes one thing prior in the case just described? I answer: simply that it is established or exists, whether in a direct or a figurative sense.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00741

The second further kind is priority through the Real, and posteriority through Him. This is a subtle kind of priority, understood only by those with deep knowledge. They say that God has different levels of divinity, and also inner aspects that do not break His absolute oneness. In short, the existence of every necessary cause comes before the existence of its essential effect in this way. Philosophers define an active cause as something that acts on something distinct from itself. So the cause's own being comes before the effect's being through causation.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00742

But the priority of existence over existence is another kind. Here, there is no action and response, no acting and being acted on. The two are like one thing with different aspects and states, moving from one state to another. What marks this kind of priority is the divine aspect. Once you understand the meaning of each kind of priority, you will also understand its opposite—posteriority—and the idea of two things being together, as these terms are understood.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00743
VI. How These Kinds of Priority Share a Meaning
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00744

People disagree about whether the word priority applies to all these kinds by name alone or by a shared meaning, and whether that meaning stays the same or changes by degree. Most later philosophers take it to have one fixed meaning in every case, without degrees. Some say that the shared meaning is this: whatever is prior, simply by being prior, has something the later thing lacks, while everything the later thing has is already present in the prior thing. This is not right. A thing that is earlier in time is gone by the time the later thing exists. Yet the time that belongs to the later thing is not present in the earlier one, nor was it present there before. The time belonging to the earlier thing is likewise never present in the later thing. Each part of time has its own existence, unlike every other part. Nor is it true without qualification that the later thing has nothing the earlier thing lacks. Later created things can have many features that the first created thing does not have, such as possibility and being a substance. The definition should at least be limited to whatever makes one thing prior. Even then, it is refuted by what we have said about parts of time and other cases.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00745

Others say that all kinds of priority share this feature: the prior thing has something that makes it more entitled to priority than the later thing. This is not right either. There is nothing in an earlier thing that makes it more entitled to be earlier than a later thing. If we compare them with some unspecified time, neither is more entitled than the other. If we compare them with their own particular times, those times are different, so they cannot both have the same one in which to be more entitled. Nor can we say that one has this advantage because of its priority, since we are trying to explain what priority means. Suppose we compare two things that are earlier and later in time. The first is earlier in every respect, and the second later in every respect. There is no third thing in this comparison. If instead we compare both with a third thing, one may be earlier than the other, but both are still earlier than the third; one is not earlier while the other is later. Besides, both definitions take for granted the general idea of priority that they are meant to explain.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00746

Some people say the word is used in completely unrelated senses. But Avicenna's discussion in The Healing suggests that one meaning applies to all the kinds by degree, while in some cases the word may also have been transferred to a new use or used figuratively. He says that people first used “before” and “after” for place and time. Then they extended “before” to anything nearer to a chosen starting point. This could be a natural order, or a chosen arrangement based on craft, luck, or chance. They then extended it to excellence and to anything that comes first even without being better. The shared idea is that the first has something the other lacks, while the other has only what the first has. A master or leader is called “before” a servant or follower in this way: the right to choose belongs to the leader, not the follower, and the follower chooses only after the leader, acting on the leader's choice.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00747

They then applied the word to relations involving existence. One, for example, can exist without many things, while many things cannot exist without one. This does not mean that one gives existence to many. Rather, many things need one so they can exist as a whole made up of parts. Finally, they used it for cases where two things have separate sources of existence, but the existence of the second comes from the first. The first then gives the second a necessity it does not have in itself; in itself, the second is only possible. In this way, the first is prior through necessity, as the movement of a hand is prior to the movement of a key.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00748

The Illuminationist author says in Al-Muṭāraḥāt that priority applies to some kinds in one shared meaning, and to others by a shared word or figuratively. The genuine kinds, he says, are priority in itself and priority by nature. Both mean that the essence of one thing comes before the essence of another. A cause, whether complete or incomplete, must come before its effect in essence and existence, so priority has one meaning in these two cases.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00749

Priority in time is the most familiar kind in ordinary speech. But when we call one person earlier than another, what we first mean is that one person's time comes before the other's. He says he has shown in this book that the priority of one time over another is by nature alone: time cannot come before time through time, since time has no other time. The relation between two times is therefore natural; when applied to two people, it is figurative.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00750

Positional rank may seem to be about place, but time also plays a part. Hamadan does not come before Baghdad by its own nature or simply by its place. It comes first for someone traveling from Khorasan to the Hejaz, because that traveler reaches it earlier in time. Natural rank works in the same way: one end of a series comes first only because someone chooses a starting point. If they start at the lower end, the higher end becomes later. The starting point is not a place; it is the time when the traveler begins. So time is involved in rank, and priority in time returns to priority by nature, as we have seen.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00751

Priority by excellence is either figurative or a case of unrelated word meanings. It is figurative when an honored person is given the first place at a gathering or allowed to begin an event. The comparison then comes down to place or time, and place itself relates to time. If that is not what is meant, then “priority” is simply a different word used for excellence. Anyone who says the word applies to all the kinds only through unrelated meanings is mistaken.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00752

The Illuminationist author concludes that the only genuine priority is priority by causation, whether it is called natural or essential. I see several problems with his account. First, it is not right to say that priority and posteriority between parts of time are only natural priority. As we have learned, priority in time means that the earlier and later things do not exist together. Natural priority does not require them to be separate in this way. These are different kinds, though one thing can be prior in two ways for two different reasons. A preparatory cause, for example, comes before its effect in time because it does not exist together with the effect, and by nature because the effect depends on it. Someone could also question whether an earlier time is naturally prior to a later one, even if the times follow one another by nature; the two ideas are different.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00753

Second, his claim that time cannot come before time because there is no time for time is not convincing. Time renews and changes through its own nature; it does not need some separate event to make it change. Other things need time in order to change, just as an essence exists through existence while existence exists without needing another existence. There are many similar examples: size in a measurable thing, number in a collection, and whiteness in what is white.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00754

Third, it is not right to say that priority by nature and priority by causation have one meaning, even if they share something, as some say all kinds do. Each kind has its own feature that makes one thing prior and another later. In priority by nature, the relevant feature is existence itself. One can exist without many, but many cannot exist unless one exists first. Existence is what makes one prior to many, or a part prior to a whole. Many times the one exists without the many; the many never exist without the one. I do not mean that one and many are equal because of their descriptions as part and whole. They are alike in receiving existence through their relation to one another. That is why Avicenna defined priority as what does not reverse in existence.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00755

In priority by causation, the relevant feature is existence in its necessity and actuality, not merely existence itself. A cause and its effect exist together, but they are not equally necessary: the cause must exist, and the effect is necessary only once the cause exists. The effect's necessity comes from the cause's necessity. In natural priority, by contrast, the difference lies in existence itself. This is another kind of priority. Yet both, together with posteriority, may be grouped under the broader name “essential priority,” because both involve a difference in existence, whether in existence itself or in how firmly it is established. Those who say that a maker causes the essence of a thing, rather than its existence, add another kind: priority by essence. Here the maker's essence is established before the essence of what it makes. They can group all three kinds under essential priority, if they use that term broadly enough to cover differences in existence and the relation between a feature and what bears it.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00756

The feature that makes one thing prior to another must be what differs between them. Since priority and posteriority are relational ideas, their kinds differ according to the things to which they are related.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00757

Fourth, it is not right to treat priority by excellence as figurative or as an unrelated use of the word. Here, too, there is a feature that can vary by degree: excellence or lack of excellence. Whiteness, knowledge, leadership, vice, goodness, and badness can all be greater or lesser. A brighter white is prior to a weaker white as white; someone more vicious comes before someone less vicious in vice. The feature that makes one prior is not existence, necessity, time, place, or rank. This kind should clearly be counted as its own kind of priority.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00758
VII. Whether Priority Changes by Degree Across Its Kinds
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00759

It is clear that the meaning of priority varies by degree when we compare its different kinds in general. It is harder to prove that this holds between every pair of kinds, and the issue is not very important. Philosophers have said that priority by causation comes before priority by nature, which comes before the other kinds; priority in time comes next, followed by priority in place.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00760

Bahmanyār says in Al-Taḥṣīl that all kinds except priority by nature and by causation are not genuine priority. Priority in time, he says, exists in thought and assumption, because time has no actual parts, only parts we imagine by dividing it. But this does not mean that time priority is not a kind of priority, as the author of Al-Muṭāraḥāt thought. It means that time is one reality outside the mind, not actually divided into parts. Where there are no actual parts, there is no real priority between them in the outside world. Yet this does not make time priority a different kind in name only. The same is true of priority by nature between parts of time: it too exists only in thought, Bahmanyār says.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00761

The truth is that the difference between parts of time belongs to their changing existence in the world, regardless of what anyone thinks or imagines. The mind can judge that one part comes before another because, outside the mind, time's parts exist in an order. They are not actual parts with separate existence, but they are very close to being parts, as in other cases where the mind describes things based on the world outside us. The evenness of four and the sky's being above the earth are examples. This does not mean that the parts of time lack a shared nature. What makes them alike is also what makes them differ, as with existence itself.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00762

This also answers the objection that priority and posteriority are relative pairs and so must exist together. How, then, can one part of time come before another? We reply that both the earlier and later parts exist together within the one continuous flow of time. Its unity is also its division, and its priority is also its presence. This is because time has a weak kind of existence and an incomplete unity.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00763
VIII. Kinds of Being Together
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00764

The kinds of being together correspond to the kinds of priority and posteriority in meaning, not in existence. Being together is not the other member of a relative pair with priority and posteriority, so it does not have to exist wherever they do. It is instead like the absence of a feature that something could have. Two things can lack priority in time without existing together at the same time; nor does the absence of natural priority mean that they are together by nature. Things entirely separate from matter have neither temporal priority nor temporal togetherness. The relation of such a thing to a person like Zayd is neither priority nor posteriority nor togetherness in time. Things that exist together in time must both be temporal, just as things that share a position or place must both be spatial. Whatever does not exist in time has no temporal priority, posteriority, or togetherness.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00765

Likewise, two things are together in essence only if they are both effects of one cause. If neither depends essentially on the same cause nor one on the other, they are not together in essence and have no priority or posteriority in that sense. Things that are together by nature may be relative pairs. Since each depends on the other, they must also depend on one cause, as explained elsewhere. So things that are together by nature are either produced by one cause, or are kinds under the same wider kind, or the like. They may depend on each other for their existence, as brothers do. Or they may not, as with kinds under one wider kind: they are together by nature because neither comes before the other in its nature. They may also be together in rank if both are naturally later than the wider kind, or they may not be.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00766

Two things can exist together in time in every respect. They cannot share a place in every respect. Bodies can match in one spatial relation: two people, for example, may be equally far from someone approaching from in front or behind. But they must differ in their relation to someone approaching from the right or left. Two bodies cannot share a place in every respect without one coming before the other in time. And some simple universal bodies cannot be together in place at all.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00767

A cause must be together with its effect because they are relative to one another. This togetherness does not cancel the priority of the cause's essence over the effect's essence. Even if they are present together as cause and effect, this does not mean that their very existence is simultaneous in the same way. The relation necessarily follows from their being cause and effect. The cause is prior to the effect in this respect.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00768

A cause cannot exist without its effect also existing. I do not mean merely that the two are relative pairs. Their existence must actually be together. If the cause is enough by itself to be a cause, then as long as it exists, it is a cause and the effect exists. If it needs something in addition to itself, then while it is only in that state, it is a cause only potentially; it does not yet have to produce an effect. The true cause is then the thing together with what must be added to it. That extra condition may be a choice or desire, or something separate that the cause awaits. Once that condition is present and nothing else is lacking, the effect must exist. The two then exist together in time, in the timeless order, or in some other way. But they are not together in the way their existence is constituted: the effect's existence depends on the cause's existence, while the cause's does not depend on the effect. It follows that removing the cause removes the effect, but removing the effect does not require that the cause be removed. The cause must be removed before its effect can be removed. Removing or restoring the cause brings about the removal or restoration of the effect. By contrast, removing or restoring the effect is a sign that the cause has been removed or restored. The effect exists with its cause and through its cause; the cause exists with the effect.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00769
IX. What Essential Coming-to-Be Really Means
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00770

If this coming-to-be describes existence, it means that existence itself depends on something else in its very identity, not through some added feature. Its very being is such that, if we set aside the existence that supports and brings it about, it would be nothing at all. It is therefore poor in itself: its very identity depends on something included in what it is, while that other thing does not depend on it, since it is rich and independent. This is one kind of “after”: existence after existence, even if both occur at the same time or in the timeless order.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00771

If coming-to-be describes an essence, it does not mean that the essence depends on something else when we ignore its existence. Meanings and essences considered without existence have no relations of dependence, priority, or posteriority. Nor does an essence, considered simply as itself, demand that it be connected to anything else. Rather, its coming after nonexistence means this: if we consider the essence just as it is in itself, it is not existent. This is a simple denial; it does not mean that a positive state of nonexistence belongs to the essence at that level. When we consider an essence in this way, both existence and nonexistence are denied of it. So are all other ideas, except the idea of the essence itself. Every simple denial is true except the denial of the essence itself; every positive claim is false except the claim that it is itself. The essence, considered as itself, is only itself. This does not mean that both sides of a contradiction are false. The opposite of “this thing exists at that level” is “this existence is denied at that level.” The qualification belongs to the existence being denied, not to the denial. The two meanings are different. Nor does reality lack one side or the other: what is real is existence, as we have shown. Existence is what truly exists, is real, is made, and comes to be. Essence exists only in a secondary sense, as something derived from existence. It is empty of everything, and even of the opposite of everything.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00772

What belongs to a thing in itself comes before what it receives from another. Every possible thing is therefore “not” in itself, then “is” through its cause. The simple “not” belongs to it in its own nature; the actual “is” belongs to it because existence is given by its cause. So its condition in itself comes before its condition as dependent on something else. This earlier state, which remains as long as the essence remains, is its essential coming-to-be. We will show that this priority and posteriority are not a separate kind, as some learned thinkers thought, but belong to priority by nature.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00773

Al-Dawānī explains Avicenna's statement that every effect is an “is after a not” in response to an objection. The objection is that an effect is no more, in itself, entitled to be nonexistent than to be existent, since it needs a cause for either state. Al-Dawānī says that because an effect's existence comes after its cause's existence, in the rank of the cause's existence the effect has only nonexistence; otherwise it would not come after the cause. But this explanation faces the same problem we discussed earlier. The fact that an effect's existence comes after its cause means only that the effect is not existent in the cause's rank. It does not mean that the effect is nonexistent there.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00774

I say that this explanation is wrong, but not for the reason just given. Since the effect's existence comes from the cause, which gives it its actuality, form, and source of being, how can we say that in the cause's rank the effect has only nonexistence? The truth is that the cause's existence is the fullness, strength, completion, necessity, and actuality of the effect's existence. What belongs to the effect as lack, limitation, and possibility is not in the cause. This is how we should understand Avicenna's words: the effect is not an “is” in itself, but it is an “is” from its cause. Every possible thing is made up of two sides: existence and actuality come from the cause; nonexistence and possibility come from the thing itself. The second side is absent from the cause.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00775

Someone may ask: if the effect does not exist at the rank of the cause, then it must be nonexistent there, or else there would be a third option. Also, nonexistence means the absence of existence. So if the effect's existence is absent at that rank, it must be nonexistent there. I reply that the opposite of “it exists at that rank” is the simple denial of that existence. It is not the positive claim that “its nonexistence exists at that rank.” The first denies a qualified existence; the second makes a qualified claim about nonexistence. Denying the first does not establish the second. It is possible that neither existence nor nonexistence is attributed to the effect at that rank, as with things that have no cause-and-effect relation. Neither their existence nor their nonexistence comes before or after the other's existence.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00776

I say that if existence is not affirmed of an essence at a certain rank, then a simple denial of existence is true there, as we have said. This does not mean that the essence has the positive feature “its existence is denied,” because that would require the essence to exist as a subject. Just as all simple denials are true of things that do not exist, and all positive claims about them are false, so too with an essence considered apart from existence and nonexistence. Simple denials are true, and positive claims are false. This does not make both sides of a contradiction false or make them disappear.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00777

As for things that have no relation of cause and effect, if one could exist only through the existence of the other, it would have the same kind of priority over it: priority by nature. The same holds for the relation between an essence and its existence. An essence is connected to existence because it can be described as existing later. If it is not first described as existing and only later as existing, then it has a kind of priority over its existence.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00778

The remaining question is whether the absence of one thing in the rank of another is enough to make the other prior, when the other has no presence in that rank. An essence has no presence before existence, so how can we say that it comes before existence? Our answer is that the mind's act of setting an essence apart from its existence—and from all other kinds of existence—is itself a kind of existence for it in reality. In this way, the essence comes before the existence it has when considered without that act of setting it apart. The same consideration both separates the essence from existence and joins it to existence. We do not say that this separation is a state the essence has in that earlier rank. We say that the separation itself is a kind of presence for the essence. To be an essence from which all existence is denied in that rank is itself a kind of being and existence. Likewise, considering it as itself alone, neither existent nor nonexistent, gives it a kind of standing. This is because existence is the source of everything. Without existence, there is no essence at all. When a cause gives something existence, the mind can consider the meaning and essence of that existence separately, since existence is incidental to the essence. Anything that has a feature incidentally can be considered before that feature.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00779

The mind can therefore analyse one existing thing into essence and existence, even though outside the mind there is only one thing. Once analysed into two, each is distinct from the other but can also be joined to it. This gives the essence a kind of priority when we consider it in this way. In reality, however, existence comes before essence in another sense: priority in reality, as we explained earlier.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00780

The result of this discussion, the scholar says, is that in the earlier rank a possible thing has only the possibility of existence and nonexistence. In that rank, it is nonexistent only in the sense that it is possible to exist or not exist. If that is enough to establish essential coming-to-be, the argument is complete; if not, it is not.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00781

I say it is surprising that he admits that the thing has the possibility of existence and nonexistence in that rank. Possibility is a negative idea: it means that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary. So he has admitted that this lack of necessity belongs to the essence in itself. This must involve some kind of presence. We now have everything needed for priority: the prior thing has some presence in that rank, while the later thing is absent from it. The essence has a presence there, as do its defining features. How could it not? The essence, considered in itself, cannot be separated from its own nature and essential features. It therefore has a kind of presence through itself, even if, in reality, that presence depends on existence, as we have explained.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00782
1. A Difficulty and Its Solution
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00783

The objection is that if the nonexistence of an essence comes before its existence, it must come before it by nature. Philosophers recognise only two kinds of essential priority: priority by causation and priority by nature. It cannot be priority by causation here. This would mean that no simple complete cause could exist, contrary to their view. They suggest this answer: a cause is whatever an effect needs in order to exist. The need itself, and what comes before that need—such as possibility and the related considerations—are outside the cause, because they are not being considered in this definition. For this reason, they explicitly say that essential possibility is not part of the cause.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00784

I say that this answer is very weak. The parts of an essence, such as its broader kind and the feature that distinguishes it, or matter and form, may be taken for granted when we discuss an effect's need for a cause. Yet these parts still count among the causes of the essence's existence. The same must be true of earlier stages before an essence exists. So it makes sense to say: it was possible, so it needed a cause, and then it came to exist. The “so” between each step points to a causal link. Philosophers also say that possibility causes a possible thing to need a cause, just as the capacity to receive causes something to be ready to receive existence and actuality. The cause must therefore be made up of parts.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00785

The sound answer is this: bringing existence itself from a cause is one thing; making an essence exist is another. As we have said, existence is what truly exists, while essence exists through it. Bringing existence from its maker does not require an essence, possibility, or any extra condition. It depends only on the being of the agent. So some things can have a simple cause: the agent's existence itself, without any condition of matter, form, essence, capacity, or possibility. But for an essence to be made existent, the cause must be composite. Since the existence being made is a state of the essence, it must come after the essence itself, its possibility, and its capacity to receive that state. There is no simple cause in this case. At the very least, the complete cause must include three things: the agent's being, the essence of what receives existence, and its capacity to receive it.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00786

This capacity for existence can also be near or far. If we consider an essence's possibility in itself, without relating it to its cause, it is a distant capacity. If we consider it in relation to its cause, it is near to becoming actual. Here, becoming actual means existing, as when prime matter receives a form and becomes one thing with it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00787
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00788

Among the features of things simply as they exist, which do not require a special natural or learned ability, are knowing, being knowledge, and being known. So knowledge and its aspects belong in first philosophy, which studies the general features of existence itself. This discussion has three parts. The first concerns what knowledge is and the features that belong to it by nature; it contains several chapters.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00789
I. Defining Knowledge
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00790

Knowledge may be one of those realities whose existence is the same as what they are. Realities of this kind cannot be defined, because definitions are made from broader kinds and distinguishing features, which are general ideas, while each existence is individual in itself. Nor can knowledge be given a complete description. Nothing is clearer than knowledge: it is an inward experience that every living, knowing being first finds in itself, without confusion or doubt. Something so clear cannot be explained by anything clearer. Since everything appears to the mind through knowledge, how could knowledge itself appear through something other than knowledge?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00791

Some things that are clear in themselves still need reminders and explanations. These help a person notice what they have overlooked, gather up the meaning, and make it clearer. Existence is like this: it is the clearest of things, yet people may still need help noticing it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00792

Some scholars argue that knowledge needs no definition because anyone who knows something can also know, without proof or reasoning, that they know it. Knowing that you know means knowing that your own self has knowledge. And knowing that one thing has a feature requires knowing both—the thing and its feature. If knowledge of knowledge had to be learned, we could not know that we know something without reasoning. But we can. So knowledge of knowledge must be immediate, not learned through proof.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00793

This argument does not show that everyone knows the full nature of knowledge. It shows only that everyone knows it in some way, without distinguishing it from other things. To know that one thing has a feature, you need only have some idea of the thing, the feature, and their relation. Logic explains that a judgment requires an idea of what is being discussed, an idea of what is said about it, and an idea of the link between them. Everyone knows they have hearing, sight, hands, feet, and a head. Most people do not know what these things are in their full nature or through a precise description.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00794
II. Why Knowing Things That Are Absent from Us Requires Their Images to Be Present in Us
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00795

In our earlier discussion of existence, we showed that things have images in the mind, especially things that do not exist—and even things that cannot exist. We make true, positive judgments about them. For example, we judge that a partner to God is impossible, that two contradictions cannot be true together, and that a mountain of gold or a sea of quicksilver would be a material substance, even though no such thing exists outside the mind. For a judgment that one thing has a feature to be true, the thing being judged must exist in some way in the setting where the judgment is made. These things, then, have existence in some mode. They cannot be described in the outside world as impossible or nonexistent there. A thing does not exist until its existence is necessary; once it exists, it is no longer nonexistent. So what is true of nonexistence and impossibility can be true only in knowledge, not in the outside world.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00796

Here is an objection: if judging something impossible means that it cannot exist, then the mental images of possible things would also be impossible to exist outside the mind. These images are the very essences of the things, and they cannot exist outside the mind in that form. This would leave no difference between what is possible and what is impossible: neither could exist outside the mind in its own way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00797

The answer is that considering an essence in itself is different from considering it as existing. An essence as it exists in the mind cannot also exist outside the mind, whether it belongs to a possible thing or not. Likewise, an essence considered with the condition of existing outside the mind cannot exist in the mind. Mental existence and outside existence cannot turn into one another. But this does not mean that an essence, considered in itself, cannot be described as existing in either way. When the mind judges an essence possible or impossible, the essence must be present in the mind. But the judgment concerns the essence in itself, not the essence as it exists in the mind. Another sign that there is a realm of knowing, where things appear to us, is that many things are truly described as shared, general, kinds, or broader kinds, even though none of these features exists in the outside world. So things must have another realm and another way of existing, where they can be general and have similar features.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00798

Strong evidence for this realm comes from what happens when the senses receive heat or cold. The images that appear in the senses are not themselves the kinds of heat or cold that we feel in the body. They belong to another of the four kinds of quality. If the strong image of heat in the sense of touch were itself something we could touch, the person touching it would feel what is in the sense organ. The same is true of taste. The strong sweetness a person senses through the tongue is not an outside sweet thing located in the tongue. If it were, anyone who ate that tongue would taste the same sweetness. These images that are present to the senses are mental qualities, features of the soul rather than the body. Mental heat is not the same kind of thing as heat outside the mind; otherwise it would burn. It is a quality of the soul.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00799

The same is true of mental cold and color, and of letters and sounds we hear inwardly, as in silent speech. If these were audible qualities, they would have to exist in struck or vibrating air. Then every person with normal hearing would hear our inner speech. These examples show us that sensible things have another kind of existence, one that is not itself sensed. They point to a realm beyond bodies and their features.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00800

Those who deny that this knowing presence differs from outside existence raise objections. They say that if outside things existed in our minds, then black and white would exist together whenever we imagined them. They also say that if essences such as a human being, the heavens, or the earth were imprinted in the mind, they would be individual images in one particular mind and so would have to exist outside the mind. If these images had the same essence and features as outside things, they would have to show the same effects: heat would burn, a human being would move, grow, and write, and blackness would make the eyes contract. But they do not. If the images did not have the same essences as outside things, then one thing could not have two kinds of existence, which is what we are trying to establish. They also argue that if knowing things meant that those things existed within us, the soul would be both moving and still, hot and cold.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00801

We answered these objections at the start of this book. Knowing things has a mode of existence distinct from their material existence. When an essence exists in this knowing mode, it loses many features and effects that belong to it in matter, including opposition, mutual exclusion, and crowding.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00802

Some people answer that a thing's features may differ according to what receives it. Heat may take on certain features when it exists in physical matter, and lack those features when it exists in a soul that has no position or size, while remaining the same essence in both cases. But this does not answer the objection if the problem concerns heat itself—its warmth and its power to burn. The answer does not explain why those features disappear. We must use the account we have already laid out for mental existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00803
III. The Proposed Accounts of Knowledge and What They Share
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00804

Many people say that the philosophers' accounts of intellect and what it understands are deeply confused. They point out that Avicenna speaks of understanding in several different ways. At times, he treats it as something negative: when he explains that God's being intellect and understood does not add anything to His being or His attributes, he says that it means He is free of matter, which is a lack of something. At other times, he describes understanding as images present in the intellect, matching the essences of the things understood. He says that for a thing to understand itself is for its image to be present to itself. In The Pointers, he says the same: to perceive something is for its reality to be present to the one who perceives it. At still other times, he treats understanding as a relation. He says that the simple intellect of the Necessary Being is intellect not because many images exist within Him, but because those images flow from Him, so that the simple intellect is like the source that creates distinct images.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00805

When the simple, unified intellect is present in us, it can likewise be the source from which our particular kinds of knowledge arise. Avicenna also describes knowledge as a quality that relates to an outside object. He says that knowledge is a feature of the soul, a quality in itself and a relation only in an indirect sense. He also says that when the known thing changes, knowledge changes, because it is a quality related to that thing.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00806

The Illuminationist author, Suhrawardi, says that knowledge is appearance, and that appearance is the very reality of light. Light may shine by itself, or it may shine on something else. If it shines by itself, it is aware of itself. If it shines on something else, that other thing may or may not shine by itself. If it does not, it may be dark in itself, or it may shine on something else, or it may not shine at all but be darkness for something else. In the first case, that other thing perceives the light. In the other three cases, it does not perceive the light and is not aware of itself. This is the core of Suhrawardi's view: a thing knows itself by being light to itself, and knows something else through a relation of light between two things that are both light.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00807

These accounts seem to contradict one another. But they can be understood as different ways of describing one view: knowledge is an existence free of matter, an existence from which material coverings have been removed.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00808

If this free existence belongs to itself, it understands itself. If it belongs to something else, as in the case of physical qualities, it understands that other thing—or imagines or senses it. This is the general meaning of knowledge. We will now challenge what the different accounts seem to say, build the view we take to be true, and then, as far as possible, show how the other accounts can be understood in line with it.
